title: Onion Rings
subtitle: Beer-battered fried onion rings
excerpt: Beer-battered onion rings are thick slices of sweet onion dipped in a cold, light batter made with beer and fried until the coating is golden and crisp. The beer gives a slight savouriness and its carbonation keeps the batter airy rather than doughy.
sourceNotes: Beer-battered onion rings are a classic American diner and fast food side dish. The beer batter became the standard because it gives a lighter, crispier result than plain flour batter.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the batter up to an hour ahead and keep cold. Fry the onion rings just before serving.

content.text: Beer-battered onion rings are a beer-and-flour batter poured over thick onion rings and deep-fried until the coating puffs and crisps. The batter should be cold, which creates steam when it hits the hot oil and gives the rings their characteristic lightness. The onion inside softens completely and turns sweet. Serve immediately, they lose their crispness quickly.

items.prepNote: peeled, cut into 1.5 cm rounds, rings separated

content.text: Make the batter and prepare the rings

Whisk {{plain-flour}}, {{cornflour}}, {{baking-powder}}, {{paprika-smoked}}, and {{sea-salt-fine}} together in a large bowl. Pour in the cold {{beer-lager}} and whisk until just combined, a few small lumps are fine; overmixing develops gluten and makes the batter tough. Refrigerate for 30 minutes.
Dust the {{white-onion}} rings in a light coating of plain flour and shake off the excess. The flour gives the batter something to grip.

Heat {{vegetable-oil}} to 180°C. Dip each floured ring into the batter, let the excess drip for a second, and lower into the oil. Fry in batches of three to four for three to four minutes, turning once, until golden and crisp. Drain on kitchen paper and season with sea salt flakes while still hot. Serve immediately.

items.symptom: The batter is thick and doughy, not crisp
items.cause: Batter too thick, overmixed, or beer too warm.
items.fix: The batter should be the consistency of thin cream. The beer must be cold. Overmixing develops gluten; mix until just combined.

items.symptom: The batter falls off in the oil
items.cause: Rings not dusted in flour first, or too much excess batter dripping off.
items.fix: Dust in flour, then dip in batter. Hold each ring over the bowl for a second to let excess drip off before lowering into the oil.

items.symptom: The rings are greasy and heavy
items.fix: At 180°C, the batter sets and crisps before it absorbs oil. Below this temperature, the batter absorbs oil and the ring becomes greasy. Don't add too many rings at once, which drops the temperature.

items.symptom: The onion slides out of the batter ring when eating
items.cause: Onion contracted during frying, separating from the batter.
items.fix: This happens with very thick-cut rings. Cut to a maximum of 1.5 cm. Thinner cuts hold together better.

content.text: Onion rings are one of the defining dishes of the American diner, alongside burgers and milkshakes. The beer batter version became standard at American pubs and restaurants as a more refined alternative to the soft, floured version served at fast food chains. Serve with ketchup, ranch dressing, or BBQ sauce.
